# Session 7: Prompt Design — Zero-shot vs Few-shot

## 📋 Agenda

- The **anatomy** of a prompt — four elements
- **Zero-shot vs. few-shot**, and **chain-of-thought**
- The wider **design space** — what to *run* vs. what to *know about*
- Two traps: **contamination** and the **validation/test split**

Our worked example all session: **Huang & Mizumoto (2025)** — writing-feedback prompts.

## 🎯 Learning Objectives

By the end of this session, you will be able to:

- **Name the four prompt elements** — *instruction · context · input data · output indicator* — and locate each in a real prompt.
- Distinguish **zero-shot** from **few-shot** prompting, judge **when examples help**, and read a real results table (Kim & Lu, 2024) to see what each contributes and where prompting stops improving.
- Explain **chain-of-thought** and which tasks it improves.
- Decide whether a technique is one to **run this week** or one to **know about**.
- Explain the **train/test contamination** trap and why you **tune on validation, report on test**.

::: {.callout-note}
The message of the day: *a prompt has parts you can design, and small changes to those parts change the score.*
:::

# The anatomy of a prompt

## A prompt has parts you can design

An LLM does what the **prompt** tells it to. Change the prompt and you change the output, and the score.

. . .

A prompt is not a fixed phrase that you either know or do not know. It has **parts you can design deliberately**, and today we learn those parts on one concrete example.

## Four elements of a prompt {.smaller}

Chen et al. (2023), via **Huang & Mizumoto (2025)** — an effective prompt typically has four parts:

- **Instruction** — what the model should *do* (start with a verb: *classify, summarize, explain*).
- **Context** — the background, role, rubric, or level that scopes the task.
- **Input data** — the actual text to be processed.
- **Output indicator** — the *form* of the answer (format, tone, "only feedback, no rewrite").

. . .

If one of the four is missing, the output is usually not what you wanted.

## Sharpening the instruction — structure & persona {.smaller}

The *instruction* element has the largest effect, so write it carefully:

- **Start with a verb and be specific** — "classify this sentence into one CEFR level (A1–C2)" is more effective than "tell me about this sentence."
- **Give it a persona / role** — *"You are an experienced EFL writing tutor…"* sets the tone, standards, and vocabulary of the output.

. . .

A persona helps, but it changes *style*, not knowledge. The **four elements** have the larger effect.

## The running example — writing feedback {.smaller}

**Huang & Mizumoto's Example Prompt 2** — a structured paragraph-feedback prompt for an EFL class:

> **Task** — Based on the following criteria, review the following paragraph and provide specific feedback… **I am not seeking rewrite, give me only feedback.**
>
> **Criteria** — 1. Hook / Attention-grabber · 2. Background / Context · 3. Thesis statement · 4. Organization · 5. Clarity & coherence
>
> **My paragraph** — *(paste your paragraph here)*

. . .

Read the four elements straight off it:

| Element | In this prompt |
|---|---|
| **Instruction** | "review… and provide specific feedback" |
| **Context** | the 5-item **Criteria** rubric |
| **Input data** | "My paragraph" |
| **Output indicator** | "only feedback, no rewrite" |

# Zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought

## Zero-shot vs. few-shot {.smaller}

- **Zero-shot** — instruction only, **no examples**. The model relies on what it already knows. Great for simple, familiar tasks.
- **Few-shot** — you include **a few worked examples** *(input → correct label)* right in the prompt, so the model infers the pattern.

. . .

**When do examples help?** When the task is specialized, the label set is your own, or the format must be exact. Two tips (promptingguide.ai):

- keep a **consistent format** across all examples;
- make the examples' **label space representative** — don't show only one class.

## What examples actually buy — Kim & Lu (2024) {.smaller}

A hard linguistic task: labelling **rhetorical move-steps** in research-article introductions (modified Swales **CARS**: 3 moves / ~17 steps) with **GPT-3.5**. Unit of annotation = the **sentence**.

. . .

They tested **two independent variables**:

- **zero-shot vs. three-shot** — the prompt alone vs. the prompt **+ 3 fully annotated introductions** (38 sentences, drawn from the **training** set — *not* the gold test set).
- **initial vs. refined prompt** — the instruction sharpened after reading the **validation-set confusion matrix**.

::: {.callout-important}
Notice: the few-shot examples come from **training**, never from the gold set you score on. (More on this shortly.)
:::

## The numbers — prompting alone stops improving {.smaller}

Test-set accuracy, **move / step** (their Table 2):


. . .

Each change helps a little, and **refined + three-shot** is best. But prompting alone reaches only about **53%** move accuracy, well below fine-tuning.

## Four things the numbers teach {.smaller}

1. **Few-shot helps, but modestly** — adding 3 examples to the *initial* prompt was **not** significant on its own (McNemar move χ²=0.543, *p*=0.46).
2. **Examples and instructions compound** — only **refined + three-shot** beat the zero-shot baseline significantly (move *p*=0.028, step *p*=0.018). Sharpen the instruction **and** add examples.
3. **Few-shot mainly raises recall** — precision was higher than recall, and examples raised recall. (That precision/recall relationship returns in S8/S9.)
4. **Context-heavy tasks need more than prompting** — the best prompt-only setting was still far below fine-tuning: prompt first, and consider fine-tuning when prompting stops improving.

::: {.callout-note}
**Discuss:** When would 3 well-chosen examples beat a longer instruction? How do you pick *which* examples to show? Why might few-shot raise recall but not precision?
:::

## Chain-of-thought (CoT) {.smaller}

Ask the model to **reason in steps** before answering (Wei et al., 2022).

**Huang & Mizumoto's Example Prompt 1** is CoT feedback:

> *First,* read the paragraph to understand its main idea. *Next,* check the structure… *Then,* identify grammatical errors. *After that,* assess clarity and coherence. **Provide feedback based on these steps.**

. . .

Zero-shot CoT is often just one added line — **"Let's think step by step"** (Kojima et al., 2022).

::: {.callout-tip}
CoT helps on tasks that need **several judgements in sequence**, such as reviewing writing or deciding a borderline label.
:::

## Iterating a prompt: Ex 1 → Ex 2 {.smaller}

The *same* feedback task, tightened:

- **Ex 1 (generic)** — "give feedback on this paragraph, step by step." Works, but vague.
- **Ex 2 (structured)** — split into **Task / Criteria / My paragraph**, add the output indicator "only feedback."

. . .

That change — generic → structured — is **prompt iteration**. The data-based version is **error analysis**: find *where* the model is wrong (the confusion matrix), make the *Criteria* that cause those errors more precise, and the score rises. This is the same as Kim & Lu's *initial → refined* change. You will do this yourself in **S9**.

# The wider design space

## Run it this week vs. know it exists {.smaller}

| **Run it in S8** | **Know it exists** (name & reason, don't run) |
|---|---|
| zero-shot | **self-consistency** — sample N answers, take the majority (relevant to reproducibility → S10) |
| few-shot | **RAG** — give the model the annotation manual / codebook to consult (≈ *dynamic* few-shot) |
| chain-of-thought | **agentic / multi-step** — the model plans → critiques its own label → revises |
| structured output | (ReAct, Reflexion, prompt chaining…) |

. . .

A reference for all of these: **[promptingguide.ai/techniques](https://www.promptingguide.ai/techniques)**.

## Two errors to avoid before you tune {.smaller}

- **Train/test contamination** — never draw your **few-shot examples from the gold set** you score on. The model would then be given the answers to the test items.
- **Validation vs. test** — **tune** the prompt on a small **validation** set; **report** the final number **once** on a held-out **test** set.

. . .

Both protect the purpose of an evaluation: **an accurate estimate of how the prompt performs on text it has not seen.**
